anchors.fact: On a Sunday afternoon in the first months of 1917, in St. Louis, Clara Bell Walsh gave the first party Oxford finds planned as and called a cocktail party. A newspaper of the time said she was "responsible for the innovation" (Oxford pdf 512).
anchors.meaning: Somebody decided a Sunday could have a new shape, and gave it a name.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: makes the fun on purpose and gives it a shape

anchors.fact: About fifty guests came, and the cocktails ran from noon to one (Oxford pdf 512; Curtis 2025 agrees on the hour).
anchors.meaning: The hour is the rule of the game: a start and an end, so anyone could join in.
anchors.speaksTo: PROVIDE STRUCTURE; gives: a way in

anchors.fact: Before that, she had tried out other party themes. One had the guests dress up as babies and drink from bottles, and it didn't last the way the cocktail party did (Oxford pdf 512).
anchors.meaning: The tally. The one that didn't take is on record, and it came first.
anchors.speaksTo: hides: the list of flops; fear: being the one who couldn't lift it

anchors.fact: Among the drinks on offer were a few Sazeracs (and Mint Juleps) for the older guests set in their ways (Felten's phrase, Oxford pdf 512). The page doesn't say who chose them.
anchors.meaning: "I like to think" she made sure the hardest guests to win over had something too. Signposted, always.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: even the hardest person gets something; say the kindness out loud

anchors.fact: Oxford calls her cocktail party the "enduring success" the baby theme wasn't (pdf 512). Felten, in 2007, calls the cocktail party "that most essential of American institutions" (*WSJ*, 6 Oct 2007).
anchors.meaning: The one that took is still how people gather. That's our reading: never "she started it", never "everyone copied her".
anchors.speaksTo: position: the ones that didn't take are how you found the one that did

anchors.fact: No gloom, no motive and no count of her flops are on record.
anchors.meaning: Only as "I like to think…". The tally belongs to the guest, never to her.
anchors.speaksTo: trap: stating the gloom as fact

cocktail.closingLine: Muddle the whole wheel, peel and all. Then tell the story of the one that didn't take.
method: Put the wine glass in the freezer for ten minutes.
Cut a thin wheel from an orange, about half a centimetre, and cut it into eight pieces. Leave the peel on.
Put the orange pieces and the coriander seeds in a shaker. Press them firmly with a muddler (or the end of a rolling pin) until the peel smells strongly of orange and the juice runs.
Add the gin, both vermouths and the bitters. Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
Pour it through the shaker's strainer and a small tea strainer held over the glass, so no seeds or pulp get in.
Nothing on the rim. The orange is already in it.
cocktail.name: Anyway

recipe.note: coriander is one of the usual botanicals in a London dry gin
more of the sweet than Oxford's recipe: it puts back the sugar a pour of orange juice would bring

recipe.item: fresh orange, about ½ cm thick, cut into eight pieces, peel and all
recipe.note: the peel is where most of an orange's flavour is; the thin wheel gives only a splash of juice
one of the usual flavourings in London dry gin, with a lemony note of its own; strained out before serving

recipe.item: Peychaud's bitters, recommended (or another bright-red New Orleans-style aromatic bitters)
recipe.note: the Sazerac's bitters, for the guests who'd rather have had a Sazerac

cocktail.tagline: You decide it's going to be a good night. Then you make it one.

reading.epigraph: People tried everything to fix the orange in the Bronx cocktail. This is one more try.
whoYouAre: It's a grey week, or a long wait, or a birthday nobody's quite in the mood for, and you've decided it's going to be good anyway. So you think of something: a silly game with proper rules, a theme, a time to turn up. Half the fun is that you took it seriously. People who would never start anything themselves find they've joined in, and even the one who swore they wouldn't ends up laughing.

There's a list, though, and only you have it: the ones that didn't take. The quiz nobody got into. The evening that stayed flat however hard you pushed it. Everyone else forgot them by the next morning. You didn't, because under all the fun is the thing you dread most: a gloom nobody could lift, and you the one who couldn't lift it. Here's what those nights gave people, even the flat ones. They could tell that someone wanted the evening to be good for them. That's what your fun was for all along, and it matters more than whether the game worked.
yours: Early in 1917, on a Sunday afternoon in St. Louis, Clara Bell Walsh had about fifty guests over for something new: an hour of cocktails, from noon until one. A newspaper at the time gave her the credit for the idea. It's the first party on record that was planned as a cocktail party and called one.

It wasn't her first idea. She'd tried other party themes before it, and in one of them the guests dressed up as babies and drank from bottles. That one didn't catch on. The cocktail party did, and more than a century later it's still one of the ways people get together. I'd have gone to both.

It's the cocktail party people remember. But it might never have come without the ones before it, and I like to think she knew it. It's the same with the list you keep. The flat evenings on it aren't the opposite of the good ones. They're how you learned what people will join in with, and what they won't. And among the drinks that Sunday there were a few Sazeracs, served to the older guests who were set in their ways. I like to think that was someone making sure even the hardest ones to win over had something there for them. That's you, too.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the sensation of her day, the Bronx: gin, two kinds of vermouth and orange. It was on her menu, and it was famously hard to get right. Put in enough orange juice to taste it, and the drink goes weak, so people kept trying new answers. The version I start from doesn't pour juice at all: one thin slice of orange is crushed in the shaker, peel and all, because the peel is where most of an orange's flavour is. You can taste the orange without drowning the gin. Then I added mine. A pinch of cracked coriander seeds goes in with the orange: coriander is one of the usual flavourings in London dry gin, with a lemony note of its own. And in place of the Angostura there are two dashes of Peychaud's, the Sazerac's bitters, for the guests who'd rather have had a Sazerac.

So keep the list. Just stop reading it as a record of what went wrong. Every idea on it that didn't take is part of the one that will. When something you've planned falls flat, laugh about it with them, and start planning another. Throw it anyway. I'd come to both.
